no_tips_available: No tips available yet for this screen.

employees.title: Employees — Tips
employees.description: An employee record is both an HR profile and a financial party, so salary, advances and staff loans post against them like any other ledger.
items: Saving an employee automatically creates a linked ledger named '<Name> (CODE)'. The code suffix keeps two people with the same name apart, so avoid reusing employee codes.
Phone and email stay on the employee record and are deliberately not copied to the ledger — otherwise an employee sharing a phone with a customer could not be saved.
Employment type decides which salary expense account payroll uses: permanent, temporary/intern/daily-wage, or contract/consultant.
Set a separation date only once the status is resigned, terminated or retired; an employee still on staff must not carry one.
Deleting an employee also hides their ledger, and restoring brings it back. An employee with posted accounting history cannot be permanently deleted.

chart_of_accounts.title: Chart of Accounts — Tips
chart_of_accounts.description: Use the chart of accounts to define your GL structure and (only when eligible) opening balances.
items: Choose the correct Account Type first. In this system, only Cash/Bank type accounts show the Opening section.
Opening is intended for initial setup (migration). After you go live, use Journal Entries instead of changing openings.
If you use multi-currency, confirm Currency + Rate before saving; base currency accounts should keep rate locked.
Use a clear numbering structure (e.g. 1xxx Assets, 2xxx Liabilities, 3xxx Equity, 4xxx Income, 5xxx Expenses) so reports stay readable.

account_transfer.title: Account Transfer — Tips
account_transfer.description: Move money between two accounts without affecting income/expense.
items: From Account and To Account cannot be the same.
Use the correct currency and exchange rate for the transfer date (base currency rate is fixed).
Add a clear remark (reason/reference) so bank/cash reconciliation is easy later.

journal_entry.title: Journal Entry — Tips
journal_entry.description: Use journal entries for adjustments, openings (when needed), and corrections.
items: Total Debit must equal Total Credit before you can save.
Avoid posting directly to Cash/Bank for sales/purchases if you already use Sales/Purchase modules—keep entries consistent.
Use Ledger and Bill Number fields when you want the entry linked to a customer/supplier and document reference.
If you attach a document, keep it to one clear file (invoice/receipt) for audit trail.

inventory_item.title: Inventory Item — Tips
inventory_item.description: An item is the catalogue entry. What a customer actually picks, scans and pays for is a variant of it — every item has at least one.

sections.heading: Identity
items: The code is generated automatically and identifies the item internally — it never changes.
Item type decides behaviour: a stocked item moves on-hand quantity; a service or charge does not. It cannot be changed once a transaction is posted.
Name, category, brand and unit describe the catalogue entry. Unit is the base unit everything is counted in.

sections.heading: Variants — the thing that is sold
items: SKU, barcode and price live on the variant, not the item. A simple product (a bottle of water) still has one variant — a single row holding its SKU, barcode and price.
For a product with choices (RAM, storage, colour, size), add an attribute column and one row per combination. Each row gets its own SKU, barcode and price.
Star one variant as the default — barcode scans and price lookups fall back to it when no specific variant is chosen.
The Margin % field is a helper: it fills the sale price from purchase price + margin. It is not saved.

sections.heading: Stock tracking
items: Batch / expiry tracking groups stock into delivery lots, each with its own batch number, expiry and landed cost. Permanent once a transaction is posted.
Serial tracking records every unit individually with its own serial number, cost and warranty.
Colour and size are ordinary variant attributes now — not separate tracking switches.
Which of these you see depends on the company's business type.

sections.heading: Opening stock
items: Use opening stock only for the starting balance at go-live. After that, every change goes through purchase, sale, transfer or adjustment.
Enter it per warehouse, and per variant when the item has more than one.
The opening unit price is the cost per unit — it drives the item's average cost and is written onto the stock movement.
Selecting a variant pre-fills the unit price with that variant's purchase price; adjust it if the real cost differs.

sections.heading: Accounts
items: Asset account holds the item's stock value on the balance sheet.
Income account is where its sales revenue is booked.
Cost of goods sold account is where the cost is booked when it is sold.
Costing method: batch/expiry-tracked items use FIFO; the rest use weighted average.

fast_entry.title: Fast Entry (Items) — Tips
fast_entry.description: Create many items on one screen. It asks only for the fields you need to start trading — everything else can be filled in later from the item edit form.

sections.heading: What this screen is for
items: Use it to load a catalogue quickly: name, unit, prices and — if you want — the opening stock you already hold.
It does not replace the full item form. Accounts, photo, variants, reorder levels, tracking flags and attachments are all edited there afterwards.
Rows left completely empty are skipped, so you never have to clear the spare ones before saving.

sections.heading: Typing fast
items: Arrow keys move between cells, Enter jumps to the next row, Tab to the next column.
A new row is added automatically as soon as you type in the last one.
The code and the barcode are generated for you — you never type them.
Typing a name selects the default unit; typing an opening amount selects the main warehouse. Change either whenever the row needs something else.

sections.heading: Prices and cost
items: Purchase price is what you pay the supplier; sale price is what you charge.
Final cost is what one unit really costs you once it reaches your shelf — the purchase price plus freight, duty and clearing. The opening stock and its accounting entry are valued at it.
Leave Final cost blank and the purchase price is used instead.

sections.heading: Opening stock
items: An opening amount needs a warehouse, and creates a stock movement plus a balanced opening-balance voucher.
Use it only for what you hold on the day you go live. After that, stock moves through purchase, sale, transfer and adjustment.
Batch and expiry columns appear when your business type tracks them. You can also switch them on from Column settings.

sections.heading: Column settings
items: Hide the columns you do not use — opening amount, batch, expiry, category, warehouse, prices and cost can all be turned off.
The choice is remembered in this browser only; it is never saved to the company.

fast_opening.title: Fast Opening (Items) — Tips
fast_opening.description: Record the stock you already hold, for every item that has no opening balance yet. An item leaves this list the moment its opening is posted.

sections.heading: What this screen is for
items: Opening stock is a one-time, go-live figure: what is physically on your shelves on the day you start using the system.
After this, stock only moves through purchase, sale, transfer and adjustment — never come back here to correct a quantity.
Only items with no opening yet are listed, so an item cannot be opened twice.
Leave the opening amount empty on anything you are not counting. Those rows are skipped, so you never have to delete them.

sections.heading: Filling it in
items: Arrow keys move between cells, Enter jumps to the next row, and Tab to the next column. On the expiry cell, Enter opens the calendar.
Typing an opening amount selects the main warehouse for that row; change it when the stock sits somewhere else.
Batch and expiry only accept typing on items that are tracked that way. On the rest they stay closed.
Use the search box to find one item in a long list — it filters the rows without losing anything you have already typed.

sections.heading: Cost
items: Final cost is what one unit really costs you — the purchase price plus freight, duty and clearing.
It is what the stock is valued at, and what the accounting entry is worth, so it drives the item average cost from day one.
A counted row needs a cost. Stock booked at zero shows a profit on the first sale that never existed.

sections.heading: What posting does
items: Each counted row creates a stock movement into the warehouse you chose, and a balanced opening-balance voucher: inventory is debited, opening-balance equity is credited.
Only the rows on the page you are looking at are saved. Finish a page, save it, then move to the next.
Batch and expiry are part of what identifies a stock lot, so enter them consistently — the same lot typed two ways becomes two separate stock lines.

transfer.title: Transfer (Inventory) — Tips
items: Pick the correct From Store and To Store; transfers change on-hand quantity in both.
Use the same batch/expiry details when transferring batch-controlled items so reports remain consistent.
Add remarks for internal traceability (who requested, why, and reference).

ledgers.title: Ledgers (Customers/Suppliers) — Tips
ledgers.description: Ledgers represent parties you buy from or sell to.
items: Keep names consistent and unique to avoid duplicate parties.
If you are migrating, set Opening/Old Balance carefully (debit vs credit) so statements match.
Use phone/address details to improve invoice printing and follow-ups.

owner.title: Owner — Tips
owner.description: Owners represent partners/shareholders used for equity tracking.
items: Create one owner record per partner so drawings and capital movements can be tracked separately.
Use clear remarks for initial capital, additional capital, or drawings references.

expense.title: Expense — Tips
expense.description: Record expense transactions with proper accounts and (optional) ledgers.
items: If you use multiple lines, ensure totals balance as expected (debit/credit rules).
Use Ledger when the expense is payable/receivable to a party (supplier/employee).
Attach the supporting document (bill/receipt) to simplify audits.

purchase.title: Purchase — Tips
purchase.description: Record purchases that affect inventory and supplier balance.
items: Select the correct Supplier ledger so payables and statements are accurate.
Use the correct Store; it controls where stock increases.
Check item Measure and prices; incorrect units can distort stock valuation and reports.

landed_cost.title: Landed Cost Guide
landed_cost.description: Freight, customs, insurance and other costs you paid to get purchased goods to the warehouse are added to the cost of those goods here, so you see their true cost and correct profit.

sections.heading: Before you start
items: The purchase bill must be posted. The list only shows posted bills: drafts, reversed bills and bills that already have an active landed cost do not appear. It shows the latest 100 bills only.
Post the landed cost before selling the goods. If part of that bill's stock has been sold or returned, the system refuses to post.
To split by weight or volume, first enter the weight, or the length, width and height, on the item itself.

sections.heading: Step by step
items: 1. Set the date and pick one or more purchase bills. Their items load automatically, and quantity and price cannot be changed here.
2. Choose the allocation method, the cash or bank account that paid, and the currency.
3. Under Category Breakdown, enter each cost next to its category. The total of these amounts is what gets shared across the items.
4. If a category is missing, create it with the Create button in that section. The bin icon only removes a category from this form; it does not delete it from the system.
5. Check each item's allocated amount and landed unit cost in the items table, then save. The document is saved as a draft and does not affect stock or the accounts yet.
6. Press Post. Posting updates the item's cost and average cost and books the entry: inventory is debited and the paying account is credited.

sections.heading: Which allocation method should I use?
items: By Value: dearer items take a larger share; suits insurance and customs. Example: a cost of 1000 with item A worth 6000 and item B worth 4000 gives 600 and 400.
By Quantity: every unit takes the same share; suits similar goods.
By Weight: item weight times quantity; suits freight. If an item has no weight, or items use different weight units, the system names the problem and does not save.
By Volume: length times width times height times quantity; suits container freight. The same conditions as weight apply.
Equal: every table row takes the same share, whatever its quantity or price.
Manual: you type each row's share. The total must equal the total of the costs.
Weight and dimensions are read from the item, not from its variants. If an item was bought in a larger unit, the system converts it to the item's own unit: 2 boxes of 12 count as 24 pieces.

sections.heading: Currency and rate
items: Cost amounts are in the currency you select. Item costs are always kept in the home currency, so each amount is multiplied by the rate before it is added.
Enter the rate of the day you paid. Example: 10 dollars at a rate of 70 adds 700 in home currency to the cost of the goods.

sections.heading: Document statuses
items: Draft: can be edited and deleted, and does not affect stock or the accounts. A deleted draft can be restored from Deleted Records, unless its bill has taken another landed cost in the meantime.
Posted: can no longer be edited or deleted. To correct it, reverse it and create a new one.

Reversed: the amount has been taken back out of the item costs and the entry has been reversed, dated the day of the reversal. It cannot be posted or edited again, but the bill is free for a new landed cost.

sections.heading: If the system refuses
items: Part of the stock has been sold or returned: a cost that arrives after a sale cannot be recorded here, because the sold share belongs in cost of goods sold. Ask your accountant how to record it. Reversing after a sale is refused for the same reason.
Allocation does not match: under Manual, correct the row amounts until they equal the total of the costs.
The account must be cash or bank: only a cash or bank account can be the paying account.
You do not see the Reverse button: posting and reversing are separate permissions. Ask your administrator for the permission to reverse landed costs.

sales.title: Sales — Quick guide
sales.description: A sale takes stock out of the warehouse and records the income and what the customer owes. The full guide has the details.

sections.heading: Fast entry with the keyboard
items: Enter on the customer goes to the barcode search; Tab goes to the first line.
Enter walks a line: item → variant → quantity → price → next line.
Arrow keys move between the fields of the table without changing a value.
F2 jumps to the barcode search. Ctrl+S, then Enter, saves.

sections.heading: Sale type and payment
items: Cash: the whole bill is received now into the cash/account you pick (required).
Credit: a dialog asks how much is received now; the rest stays on the customer.
On loan: nothing is received now; the whole bill goes on the customer.
The system works out the bill total from the lines, and a payment cannot exceed it.

sections.heading: Lines
items: The stock shown is the chosen variant’s stock in the chosen warehouse.
Free units are not charged but do leave the warehouse.
The expiry date is picked from the dates in stock; leave it empty to take the nearest expiry first.
Changing the currency converts every price; if the currency has no rate, type the rate and the prices follow.

sections.heading: After saving
items: A draft only reserves stock and is costed on the day it is posted.
A posted bill is locked: correct it with a reversal or a sales return.
A return credits what the customer actually paid, after discounts.

receipt.title: Receipt — Tips
receipt.description: Record money received from customers or other sources.
items: Choose the correct Cash/Bank account as the receiving account.
Use Cheque Number / reference fields for non-cash receipts.
If you see Old Balance, it helps you confirm how this receipt impacts the ledger balance.

payments.title: Payments — Tips
payments.description: Record money paid to suppliers or other parties.
items: Choose the correct Cash/Bank account as the paying account.
Use cheque/reference details for bank payments.
Double-check currency and rate to avoid balance differences.

user_management.title: User Management — Tips
user_management.description: Manage users, roles, and permissions safely.
items: Use Roles to group permissions—avoid assigning many permissions directly to each user.
Give the minimum permissions required (least privilege) to reduce mistakes and risk.
If a user can edit financial transactions, consider enabling approval/locking rules in Preferences.

preferences.title: Preferences — Tips
preferences.description: Preferences control how forms and transactions behave across the system.
items: Item Management controls which fields appear on the Item screens; hide unused fields for faster data entry.
Sale/Purchase tabs let you choose visible columns and numbering; set them before daily usage starts.
Backup/Export preferences should be configured early so data recovery is always possible.

attendances.title: Attendance — Tips
attendances.description: Attendance can be entered by hand, imported from a terminal, or clocked by employees themselves. All three write the same daily record.
items: The daily roster is the fallback that always works: pick a date and a department, and confirm the pre-filled statuses.
Importing a punch log never loses a row. Punches from a device ID nobody has mapped land on the Unmapped Punches screen — map the ID there and the days are recalculated without re-uploading the file.
Re-importing the same export is safe; duplicate punches are rejected by the database, not counted twice.
A day showing "needs review" had a single punch with no pair — usually someone forgot to clock out. Fix it on the roster rather than guessing the hours.
Once a payroll has been posted, the days it consumed are locked and can no longer be edited. Reverse the payroll first if a correction is genuinely needed.

leave_requests.title: Leave — Tips
leave_requests.description: A leave request moves draft → pending → approved, and approving it writes the leave days into the attendance register automatically.
items: Day counts are calculated from the leave type, not typed in: types that skip weekends and holidays charge fewer days than the calendar span.
Pending days are shown separately from the balance and are never deducted — nobody has agreed to them yet.
Approval is refused when the balance is short, except for unpaid leave, which is allowed to go negative by design.
Cancelling approved leave removes the future days from attendance and leaves past days alone: last week already happened.
Approving is a separate permission from editing, so raising a request on someone’s behalf does not let you grant it.

payrolls.title: Payroll — Tips
payrolls.description: A payroll run is created first and calculated afterwards. Calculating is safe to repeat while the run is still a draft.
items: Leave the scope blank to include everyone; narrow it to a department or an employment type to run payroll for part of the company.
Recalculating replaces the payslips of a draft run, so fixing a salary structure and calculating again is the normal correction.
Posting writes the run to the ledger. From that point the run is a fact: correcting it means reversing it, not editing it.
Attendance days consumed by a posted run are locked, which is why a reversal is required before the days can change.
Approving is a separate permission from editing, so preparing a run does not let you post it.

salary_payments.title: Salary payment — Tips
salary_payments.description: A salary payment settles what an employee is owed. Leaving the allocation alone applies the money oldest-first across their open payslips.
items: The outstanding list is read from the ledger, not from a cached figure, so it shows what is genuinely still open.
Choose which payslips only when the money is meant for a specific month; otherwise the oldest-first default is what people expect.
Pay all fills the amount with the full outstanding total — it does not save anything on its own.
Paying more than is outstanding leaves the remainder on account against the employee.
A payment can be voided but not edited: the ledger entry it made has to be reversed rather than restated.

employee_loans.title: Loans and advances — Tips
employee_loans.description: Approval and payout are separate steps. Approving authorises the money; it does not move it.
items: The instalment schedule must add up to the principal, and the shortfall is shown while you type rather than only on save.
Suggest divides the principal by the number of instalments and rounds up, which is usually the intended schedule.
With recovery through payroll enabled, each payroll run deducts one instalment automatically until the loan is settled.
Once the money has been disbursed the principal and schedule can no longer be edited — the ledger already carries that balance.
A repayment can also be recorded by hand, for a loan settled in cash outside payroll.

salary_structures.title: Salary structure — Tips
salary_structures.description: A structure is the salary package: a basic salary plus the allowances and deductions that sit on top of it.
items: Attach it to one employee for a personal package, or to a designation or department to use it as a grade template.
Picking a component fills in its own defaults, so the usual case is one click and no typing.
The indicative gross covers fixed amounts and percentages of basic only. Anything on a percentage of gross is not known until the payslip is resolved.
Effective dates decide which structure a payroll run uses, so raise a new structure rather than editing history.
A structure with no components is valid — it simply pays the basic salary.

barcode_print.title: Print Barcode — Tips
barcode_print.description: Lay out a sheet of barcode labels and print it. The barcode and the price come from the variant, so a product with choices prints one label per variant.

sections.heading: Choosing the paper
items: A4 and A5 tile as many labels as fit across the page; the count per row is shown under the options.
The Label kinds are for a sticker roll and are defined by their column count instead — the stock itself is that wide.
Label width and height are the sticker, not the gap. Horizontal and vertical spacing are the gaps between them.
Margins are the blank edge of the sheet. Reset puts them back to 10 mm on every side.

sections.heading: Symbology — what each one accepts
items: CODE128 is the safe default: letters, digits and symbols, any length. It encodes the codes this system generates as-is.
CODE128A drops lowercase; CODE128B takes both cases; CODE128C takes digits only, in pairs (an even count).
CODE39 takes uppercase letters, digits and - . $ / + % and space.
MSI takes digits only, any length. Codabar must start and end with A, B, C or D with only digits and - $ : . + / between.

EAN-13 (13 digits), EAN-8 (8), UPC-A (12) and ITF-14 (14) are GS1 retail standards. The last digit must be a computed check digit, and the number itself is assigned to a company by GS1 — it is not one you invent.

That is why an auto-generated code like ITM681421515 prints under CODE128 but is refused by EAN-13: it has letters, the wrong length, and no check digit. Use CODE128 for your own shelf labels, and the GS1 types only for codes printed on the manufacturer packaging.

sections.heading: Choosing products
items: The ten newest items are listed to start with. Use the search box above the table to add anything else.
Tick the rows you want, set a quantity per row, or use Number of Barcodes to set the same quantity on everything ticked.
A product with no barcode cannot be ticked — give it one on the item form first.
The filter box narrows the table without losing your ticks or quantities.

sections.heading: What prints
items: Draw Code, Name, Variant, Barcode, Price and Border each control one line of the sticker; the heading prints once at the top of the sheet.
The preview is the sheet: what you see laid out is what comes out of the printer.
Check the preview before printing a full roll — label stock is expensive to waste.

item_pricing.title: Item Pricing — Tips
item_pricing.description: Set sale prices across many products at once. Price lives on the variant, so a product with choices has one price per variant.

sections.heading: What is listed
items: The ten newest variants are shown to start with — the things most likely to still need a price. Change the page size or search to reach anything else.
A product with real choices shows one row per variant, each with its own sale price. A plain product shows a single row with no variant label.
On hand, cost and purchase price are shown for context; only the sale price and margin can be typed.

sections.heading: Setting a price
items: Type in the Sale Price box, or type a Margin % and the price is worked out from the cost.
Margin is measured against the average cost once stock has moved, and against the purchase price before that. A product with neither cannot take a margin.
A price below cost is flagged on the row. It is allowed — clearance happens — but it is never silent.
Arrow keys move between the price and margin boxes and up and down the rows.

sections.heading: Repricing a shelf at once
items: Tick the rows you want, pick a bulk action and press Apply.

Pick Increase or Decrease, then Change by % to move the current price by a percentage, or Change by amount to shift it by a fixed sum. Enter the figure as a positive number — the direction decides which way it goes.
Set margin % recalculates each price from that row own cost, so a mixed shelf ends up at one consistent margin.
Round to nearest snaps prices to a step — 5 or 10 — which is how shelf prices are usually set.

sections.heading: Saving
items: Nothing reaches the database until you press Save. Changed rows are highlighted and show old → new.
Save sends every change in one request and asks you to confirm the list first.
Revert throws away everything typed and puts the saved prices back.
Documents already posted keep the price they were saved with — repricing only affects what is sold from now on.
